newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Ericsson results show market still strong.
newsitem.headline: Ericsson results show market still strong.

text.p: Swedish telecoms group Ericsson's 1996 earnings and market growth forecast show the global mobile telephony market is still going strong, analysts said on Tuesday.

"The report was good news," Simon Street, analyst at BZW told Reuters. "The digital handset market is growing so rapidly that Ericsson could increase its market share while allowing new companies to enter the segment."
Ericsson posted a 33 percent jump in pre-tax profits for 1996 to 10.15 billion crowns and 26 percent higher sales of 124.27 billion crowns.
On Monday, the company forecast an increase in mobile phone subscribers to 480 million worldwide in 2000 from an expected 137 million at the end of 1996.
The company said digital subscribers were expected to grow 10-fold between 1996 and 2001 to 500 million from 50 million while the number of analogue subscribers peaked in 1998.
"Ericsson has constantly upgraded, not downgraded its forecasts," said Jonas Blomberg, analyst at brokerage Nordiska.
The forecast and the report were seen as of particular benefit to Finnish rival Oy Nokia, which is also strong on the digital side. Nokia is due to release its 1996 earnings report on February 13.
U.S. rival Motorola Corp is more exposed to analogue phones, analysts said.
Ericsson's deputy managing director CW Ros said the company did not see any signs of an end to price pressures in 1997.
"I would not be surprised if it was about the same as last year," Ros told a press conference.
Some analysts saw this as positive for the sector.

"That Ericsson does not see a further increase in price pressure on digital systems in 1997 is also good news for Nokia, which has 50-60 percent of production in digital handsets," said Lars Larsen, analyst at Aros brokerage.
However Motorola's shares declined three to 64-1/2 on the price pressure comments, market sources in Chicago said.
Ericsson is even more digitalised than Nokia, with roughly 90 percent of its mobile phones being digital, analysts said.
The Swedish group's report, however, was not all rosy as Ericsson said its gross margin weakened, partly following increased competition.
"You should not get your expectations up too high," Blomberg said. "But I don't see any signs of weaknesses in the report at all."
Competition on the mobile system side could, however, get tougher, he said.
"Ericsson said CDMA had two percent of the market worldwide in 1996 and it forecast the system might hold as much as 10-15 percent at the turn of the century," Blomberg said.
Of the three sector giants, Ericsson promotes Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) and Nokia mainly focuses on that system too, while Motorola favours Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA).
At the moment, TDMA dominates worldwide while CDMA mainly exists in the U.S. and South Korea.
Ericsson is the leading digital systems supplier with about 40-50 percent of the world market.
